newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks seen opening down.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks seen opening down.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open lower Monday on follow-through from the Dow industrials' 148-point decline Friday, analysts said.
"I think we'll have an easier opening," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities. "I think the key to the morning will be what happened Friday."

Investors will keep an eye on semiconductor maker Intel Corp, whose first quarter earnings are due out after the market close at 1600 EDT/1800 GMT. The results could provide direction for slumping technology stocks.
Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments, said, "Intel's earnings are going to be very crucial as far as the technology sector is concerned."
He said Wall Street should open flat to lower but that Friday's relatively low volume showed panic selling today was unlikely.
"Are we in for a Black Monday? I don't think so," he said.
Markets also will be readying for the March Consumer Price Index, due out Tuesday. Investors will be looking for signs of inflation and possible higher interest rates.
"If we get another jolt in the Consumer Price Index...the market will test this 6250 area everybody is talking about," Cardillo said. The Dow closed Friday at 6391.69.
The Atlanta Federal Reserve releases its March index at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT today. The previous report was 7.0.
In Tokyo the Nikkei Average dropped 154.51 points, or 0.87 percent, to close at 17,692.47.
In London the FTSE 100 index was off 27.2 points at 4243.5.
Light bargain-hunting lifted U.S. technology stocks in London, but most U.S. stocks were unchanged, reflecting nervousness about a falling market.
The dollar was at 126.37/43 against the yen in Tokyo. The greenback in Europe held above 1.72 marks and in the mid-126 range against the yen.
The U.S. Treasury 30-year bond was off 4/32 to yield 7.18 percent. The Standard & Poors 500 futures index was off 0.35 at 738.15.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column said Raytheon Co and other defense contractors are under attack from lawmakers who oppose federal reimbursements for restructuring costs. The Senate holds hearings this week on defense industry mergers.

The New York Times's Market Place column said damage to most U.S. stocks in the recent downturn has been more severe than the 10 percent drop suffered by the Dow Jones Industrial Average. Technology stocks have been especially hard hit.
